input.ground_truth: I would like to take a brief (and relatively naive) stab at the Navier-Stokes equations problem on an ELI5 level: In the 19th century, a physicist (Navier) first devised a set of equations to model the movement of fluids to determine their velocity (speed in a given direction) at a given point in space at a given time. These equations have been proven to accurately model fluid velocity in two-dimensional space, but not yet for three-dimensional space.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Any of the seven Millennium Prize Problems

Answer:

response.prediction: These are seven really hard math puzzles that even grown-ups can't solve. If you solve one, you get a million dollars! They're like super-duper hard games that only a few people can figure out. These puzzles are important because solving them can help us understand more about math and science, which can make the world a better place. Maybe one day you could solve one of these puzzles and help the world!

The Clay Mathematics Institute offered a million dollars for each problem solved, hence the name "Millennium Prize Problems."

But how do I break this down for a kid? Maybe I can compare them to something a child would understand, like puzzles or games. I think using an analogy would work best. So, maybe I can say that these are like super-hard puzzles that even grown-ups can't solve, and if you can solve one, you get a million dollars.

Wait, but I need to make sure I'm not oversimplifying or making it sound too easy. I don't want the child to think it's something they can just figure out in a day. Maybe I should emphasize that these are really tricky and that only a few people in the whole world can solve them.

Also, I should mention that there are seven of these problems, each one different and challenging in its own way. Maybe I can give a simple example of one of them to make it more concrete. For instance, the Riemann Hypothesis is one of them, but explaining that to a five-year-old would be tough. Maybe instead, I can say something like "one of them is about how numbers work together, and it's been unsolved for a really long time."

I also need to keep the language simple and avoid any technical terms. Words like "prize," "problems," "math," and "solve" should be okay. Maybe I can use a phrase like "big math puzzles" instead of "Millennium Prize Problems."

Another thing to consider is the child's interest. If they like puzzles or games, I can relate it to that. Maybe say, "Imagine there are seven really hard puzzles that even the smartest grown-ups can't solve. If you can solve one, you get a million dollars!"

I should also make it positive and encouraging, so the child feels inspired rather than intimidated. Maybe add something like, "These puzzles are so important that solving them can help us learn more about the world and how it works."

Okay, so here's my attempt: "These are seven really hard math puzzles that even grown-ups can't solve. If you solve one, you get a million dollars! They're like super-duper hard games that only a few people can figure out."

Hmm, that seems too short and maybe a bit simplistic. Maybe I can add a bit more detail without making it too complicated. Perhaps mention that these puzzles are important for math and science, and solving them can help us understand things better.

Alright, let's try again: "These are seven really hard math puzzles that even grown-ups can't solve. If you solve one, you get a million dollars! They're like super-duper hard games that only a few people can figure out. These puzzles are important because solving them can help us understand more about math and science, which can make the world a better place."

That seems better. It explains what the problems are, why they're important, and the reward for solving them, all in simple terms a five-year-old can grasp. I think this approach works because it uses relatable concepts like puzzles and games, and it highlights the significance and reward of solving them.

I should also make sure to use positive language to encourage the child's interest in math and problem-solving. Maybe add something like, "Maybe one day you could solve one of these puzzles and help the world!"

Okay, I think I've got a good explanation that's simple, positive, and informative for a five-year-old.
